scope: Exodus 5–6, all 53 public verses. Prior revisions remain unchanged.

source.verse_hash_method: SHA-256 of the exact original XML verse substring, including written/read notes, not a normalized substitute.
source.public_versification_note: Public and Hebrew verse numbering align throughout Exodus 5–6.

delta_method: F0 retained wording; F1 lexical; F2 syntax/idiom; F3 consequential interpretive, textual, social, or versification choice. Editorial assessments are separate from similarity scores. Independent review has not occurred.

verses.rationale: Retains both messengers, the divine speech formula, and festival as the purpose of release; preserves the recurring let-my-people-go demand.
verses.before: Afterward Moses and Aaron went in and said to Pharaoh, “Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Let my people go, so that they may hold a festival for me in the wilderness.”
verses.after: Afterward, Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Let my people go so they can celebrate a festival for me in the wilderness.’”
verses.tsw_comparator: Afterward Moses and Aaron went in and said to Pharaoh, “Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Let my people go, so that they may hold a festival for me in the wilderness.”

verses.rationale: Keeps the voice and knowing language alongside Pharaoh’s explicit refusal, without turning his challenge into a neutral request for information.
verses.before: Yet Pharaoh said, “Who is the LORD, that I should listen to his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and I will not let Israel go.”
verses.after: Pharaoh answered, “Who is the LORD, that I should listen to his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and I will not let Israel go.”
verses.tsw_comparator: But Pharaoh said, “Who is the LORD, that I should listen to his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and I will not let Israel go.”

verses.rationale: Retains a three-day journey rather than a three-day absence and preserves us as the threatened group in the messengers’ warning.
verses.before: They said, “The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Please, let us go a journey of three days into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God, lest he strike us with plague or with the sword.”
verses.after: They said, “The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Please let us travel three days into the wilderness to sacrifice to the LORD our God, or he may strike us with plague or sword.”
verses.tsw_comparator: They said, “The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Please, let us go a journey of three days into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God, lest he strike us with plague or with the sword.”

verses.rationale: Keeps the direct address and command directed at the plural hearers, with burdens continuing chapter 1’s forced-labor vocabulary.
verses.before: But the king of Egypt said to them, “Why, Moses and Aaron, do you draw the people away from their work? Go to your burdens!”
verses.after: The king of Egypt said to them, “Moses and Aaron, why are you drawing the people away from their work? Get back to your burdens!”
verses.tsw_comparator: But the king of Egypt said to them, “Why, Moses and Aaron, do you draw the people away from their work? Go to your burdens!”

verses.rationale: Follows the explicit speech verb instead of recasting the king’s words as private thoughts; retains population and interrupted labor.
verses.before: Pharaoh said, “Look, the people of the land are now many, and you would make them rest from their burdens!”
verses.after: Pharaoh continued, “Look how many people there are in the land now, and you are stopping them from carrying their burdens!”
verses.tsw_comparator: And Pharaoh said, “Look, the people of the land are now many, and you would make them rest from their burdens!”

verses.rationale: Keeps the same-day response and two levels of labor authority, with the speech continuing across the verse label.
verses.before: That same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters over the people and their foremen, saying,
verses.after: That same day Pharaoh gave orders to the people’s taskmasters and foremen:
verses.tsw_comparator: That same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters over the people and their foremen, saying,

verses.rationale: Makes the withdrawal of supplies an order, not permission, while rendering yesterday-and-before as the habitual past.
verses.before: “You will no longer give the people straw for making bricks, as before. Let them go and gather straw for themselves.
verses.after: “Stop supplying the people with straw for making bricks as you did before. They must go and gather their own straw.
verses.tsw_comparator: “You shall no longer give the people straw for making bricks, as before. Let them go and gather straw for themselves.

verses.rationale: Retains the unchanged demand and the charge of laziness as Pharaoh’s explanation, not the narrator’s judgment of enslaved workers.
verses.before: But you will require from them the full quota of bricks that they made before; you will not reduce it. For they are idle. That is why they cry out, saying, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’
verses.after: But require them to make as many bricks as before. Do not reduce the quota. They are lazy—that is why they keep crying, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’
verses.tsw_comparator: But you shall require from them the full quota of bricks that they made before; you shall not reduce it. For they are idle. That is why they cry out, saying, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’

verses.rationale: Preserves the heaviness image, male workers, and Pharaoh’s characterization of the message as lies.
verses.before: Let the work be heavy upon the men, so that they labor at it and pay no attention to lying words.”
verses.after: Make the work weigh more heavily on the men. Keep them at it so they pay no attention to lying words.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Let the work be heavy upon the men, so that they labor at it and pay no attention to lying words.”

verses.rationale: Keeps both officials and the royal speech formula that parallels the opening divine message.
verses.before: So the taskmasters of the people and their foremen went out and said to the people, “Thus says Pharaoh: ‘I am not giving you straw.
verses.after: The taskmasters and foremen went out and told the people, “This is what Pharaoh says: ‘I will give you no straw.
verses.tsw_comparator: So the taskmasters of the people and their foremen went out and said to the people, “Thus says Pharaoh: ‘I am not giving you straw.

verses.rationale: Retains the emphatic transfer of responsibility for supplies and the absolute refusal to reduce labor.
verses.before: You yourselves go, get straw wherever you can find it, for not a thing will be reduced from your work.’”
verses.after: Go and get your own straw wherever you can find it. Your work will not be reduced at all.’”
verses.tsw_comparator: You yourselves go, get straw wherever you can find it, for not a thing will be reduced from your work.’”

verses.rationale: Distinguishes the stubble actually gathered from the straw previously supplied and keeps the geographic spread.
verses.before: So the people scattered throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.
verses.after: So the people scattered throughout Egypt to gather stubble to use as straw.
verses.tsw_comparator: So the people scattered throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.

verses.rationale: Preserves ongoing pressure, daily completion, and the explicit comparison with earlier supply conditions.
verses.before: And the taskmasters pressed them, saying, “Finish your work—each day’s task on its day—as when the straw was provided.”
verses.after: The taskmasters kept pressing them: “Finish each day’s work, just as you did when straw was supplied!”
verses.tsw_comparator: And the taskmasters pressed them, saying, “Finish your work—each day’s task on its day—as when the straw was provided.”

verses.rationale: Distinguishes the beaten Israelite intermediaries from the taskmasters and retains both missed days without inventing a specific interrogator.
verses.before: The Israelite foremen, whom Pharaoh’s taskmasters had set over them, were beaten, saying, “Why have you not completed your prescribed quota of brickmaking as before, both yesterday and today?”
verses.after: The Israelite foremen whom Pharaoh’s taskmasters had put over the people were beaten. “Why have you not met your brick quota,” they were asked, “either yesterday or today, as you did before?”
verses.tsw_comparator: The Israelite foremen, whom Pharaoh’s taskmasters had set over them, were beaten, saying, “Why have you not completed your prescribed quota of brickmaking as before, both yesterday and today?”

verses.rationale: Keeps the appeal to Pharaoh and the foremen’s self-description as his servants, with the complaint continuing into verse 16.
verses.before: Then the Israelite foremen came and cried out to Pharaoh, saying, “Why do you treat your servants this way?
verses.after: The Israelite foremen went to Pharaoh and cried out, “Why are you treating your servants like this?
verses.tsw_comparator: Then the Israelite foremen came and cried out to Pharaoh, saying, “Why do you treat your servants this way?

verses.rationale: Retains the repeated self-reference and physical violence; follows the your-people-at-fault construal while flagging the difficult final Hebrew clause.
verses.before: No straw is given to your servants, yet they say to us, ‘Make bricks!’ And look, your servants are beaten, though your people are at fault.”
verses.after: Your servants receive no straw, yet we are told, ‘Make bricks!’ Look, your servants are being beaten, but the fault lies with your own people.”
verses.tsw_comparator: No straw is given to your servants, yet they say to us, ‘Make bricks!’ And look, your servants are beaten, though your people are at fault.”

verses.rationale: Preserves the doubled accusation and the repeated sacrifice request as quoted by Pharaoh.
verses.before: But he said, “You are idle, idle! That is why you say, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.’
verses.after: “Lazy!” Pharaoh said. “You are lazy! That is why you say, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.’
verses.tsw_comparator: But he said, “You are idle, idle! That is why you say, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.’

verses.rationale: Keeps both parts of the renewed order together: no supplies and no reduction in required production.
verses.before: Now go, work! Straw will not be given to you, but you will deliver the required quota of bricks.”
verses.after: Now go back to work. You will get no straw, but you must deliver the full brick quota.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Now go, work! Straw will not be given to you, but you shall deliver the required quota of bricks.”

verses.rationale: Makes the foremen’s recognition clear while preserving the daily demand’s further repetition.
verses.before: The Israelite foremen saw that they were in trouble when it was said, “You will not reduce the number of bricks—each day’s task on its day.”
verses.after: The Israelite foremen saw that they were in trouble when they were told, “You must not reduce the number of bricks required each day.”
verses.tsw_comparator: The Israelite foremen saw that they were in trouble when it was said, “You shall not reduce the number of bricks—each day’s task on its day.”

verses.rationale: Clarifies who was leaving and who was waiting without adding a purpose beyond the meeting.
verses.before: As they came out from Pharaoh, they encountered Moses and Aaron standing there to meet them.
verses.after: As they left Pharaoh, they came upon Moses and Aaron, who were standing there to meet them.
verses.tsw_comparator: As they came out from Pharaoh, they encountered Moses and Aaron standing there to meet them.

verses.rationale: Keeps both ancient images, including the mixed smell/sight expression, and the foremen’s accusation of lethal consequences.
verses.before: They said to them, “May the LORD look on you and judge, because you have made our smell foul in the eyes of Pharaoh and in the eyes of his servants, putting a sword in their hand to kill us.”
verses.after: They said to Moses and Aaron, “May the LORD look at you and judge! You have made us stink in the eyes of Pharaoh and his servants. You have put a sword in their hands to kill us.”
verses.tsw_comparator: They said to them, “May the LORD look on you and judge, because you have made our smell foul in the eyes of Pharaoh and in the eyes of his servants, putting a sword in their hand to kill us.”

verses.rationale: Preserves Moses’ direct attribution of harm to God as a complaint, without softening it to a request for reassurance.
verses.before: Then Moses returned to the LORD and said, “Lord, why have you brought harm upon this people? Why is this why you sent me?
verses.after: Moses returned to the LORD and said, “Lord, why have you brought harm on this people? Why did you send me?
verses.tsw_comparator: Then Moses returned to the LORD and said, “Lord, why have you brought harm upon this people? Why is this why you sent me?

verses.rationale: Repeats brought harm with Pharaoh now the subject and keeps the emphatic denial of rescue and your-people wording.
verses.before: For since I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has brought harm upon this people, and you have not delivered your people at all.”
verses.after: Ever since I went to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has brought harm on this people, and you have not rescued your people at all.”
verses.tsw_comparator: For since I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has brought harm upon this people, and you have not delivered your people at all.”

verses.rationale: Preserves the twice-repeated strong hand and the escalation from release to expulsion; leaves the hand unpossessed and notes the contextual agency question.
verses.before: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh. For by a strong hand he will send them away, and by a strong hand he will drive them out of his land.”
verses.after: The LORD said to Moses, “Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh. Under a strong hand he will let them go; under a strong hand he will drive them out of his land.”
verses.tsw_comparator: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh. For by a strong hand he will send them away, and by a strong hand he will drive them out of his land.”

verses.rationale: Retains the short divine self-identification as the opening of the renewed speech rather than merging it away.
verses.before: God spoke to Moses and said to him, “I am the LORD.
verses.after: God spoke to Moses. “I am the LORD,” he said.
verses.tsw_comparator: God spoke to Moses and said to him, “I am the LORD.

verses.rationale: Follows the Hebrew negative statement without silently making it a question or adding fully; keeps the established El Shaddai rendering and notes the tension with Genesis.
verses.before: I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob as God Almighty, but by my name the LORD I was not known to them.
verses.after: “I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty, but by my name, the LORD, I was not known to them.
verses.tsw_comparator: I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob as God Almighty, but by my name the LORD I was not known to them.

verses.rationale: Keeps covenant, land, and foreign residence connected rather than making the ancestors owners of the whole land already.
verses.before: I also established my covenant with them, to give them the land of Canaan, the land where they lived as resident aliens.
verses.after: I also established my covenant with them to give them Canaan, the land where they lived as foreigners.
verses.tsw_comparator: I also established my covenant with them, to give them the land of Canaan, the land where they lived as resident aliens.

verses.rationale: Retains emphatic divine hearing, explicit Egyptian enslavement, and covenant remembrance as distinct claims.
verses.before: Moreover, I have heard the groaning of the Israelites, whom the Egyptians are enslaving, and I have remembered my covenant.
verses.after: I myself have heard the groaning of the Israelites, whom the Egyptians are enslaving, and I have remembered my covenant.
verses.tsw_comparator: Moreover, I have heard the groaning of the Israelites, whom the Egyptians are enslaving, and I have remembered my covenant.

verses.rationale: Unfolds the three promises into short repeated I-will clauses while preserving burdens, slavery, redemption, arm, and judgment.
verses.before: So say to the Israelites: I am the LORD. I will bring you out from under the burdens of Egypt, and I will deliver you from their slavery. I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment.
verses.after: So tell the Israelites, ‘I am the LORD. I will bring you out from under Egypt’s burdens. I will rescue you from their slavery. I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and great acts of judgment.
verses.tsw_comparator: Therefore say to the Israelites: I am the LORD. I will bring you out from under the burdens of Egypt, and I will deliver you from their slavery. I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment.

verses.rationale: Keeps both sides of the people/God relationship, the knowing response, and the repeated burden-release description.
verses.before: I will take you for my people, and I will be your God. Then you will know that I am the LORD your God, who brings you out from under the burdens of Egypt.
verses.after: I will take you as my people, and I will be your God. Then you will know that I am the LORD your God, who brings you out from under Egypt’s burdens.
verses.tsw_comparator: I will take you for my people, and I will be your God. Then you will know that I am the LORD your God, who brings you out from under the burdens of Egypt.

verses.rationale: Retains the raised-hand oath image, all three ancestors, and possession rather than replacing the concrete promise with general blessing.
verses.before: I will bring you into the land that I raised my hand to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and I will give it to you as a possession. I am the LORD.”
verses.after: I will bring you into the land I raised my hand in an oath to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. I will give it to you as a possession. I am the LORD.’”
verses.tsw_comparator: I will bring you into the land that I raised my hand to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and I will give it to you as a possession. I am the LORD.”

verses.rationale: Renders shortness of spirit as crushed spirits in context and preserves harsh labor as a second stated cause, without blaming the people’s character.
verses.before: Moses spoke this way to the Israelites, but they did not listen to Moses because their spirit was broken and because of harsh slavery.
verses.after: Moses told the Israelites all this, but they did not listen to him because their spirits were crushed and their labor was harsh.
verses.tsw_comparator: Moses spoke this way to the Israelites, but they did not listen to Moses because their spirit was broken and because of harsh slavery.

verses.rationale: Keeps the renewed speaker attribution attached to the command in the next verse.
verses.before: Then the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,
verses.after: Then the LORD said to Moses,
verses.tsw_comparator: Then the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,

verses.rationale: Preserves speaking as the assigned action and release as its intended result.
verses.before: “Go, speak to Pharaoh king of Egypt, so that he will send the Israelites out of his land.”
verses.after: “Go and speak to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, so that he will let the Israelites leave his land.”
verses.tsw_comparator: “Go, speak to Pharaoh king of Egypt, so that he will send the Israelites out of his land.”

verses.rationale: Retains Moses’ argument from the people’s response to Pharaoh’s and preserves the uncircumcised-lips image with a concise explanation.
verses.before: Yet Moses spoke before the LORD, saying, “Look, the Israelites have not listened to me; how then will Pharaoh listen to me, since I am uncircumcised of lips?”
verses.after: But Moses answered the LORD, “The Israelites have not listened to me. How will Pharaoh listen, when my lips are uncircumcised?”
verses.tsw_comparator: But Moses spoke before the LORD, saying, “Look, the Israelites have not listened to me; how then will Pharaoh listen to me, since I am uncircumcised of lips?”

verses.rationale: Keeps both commissioned men, both parties named in the charge, and the stated task without inventing unreported instructions.
verses.before: The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them a command concerning the Israelites and Pharaoh king of Egypt: to bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt.
verses.after: The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them a charge concerning the Israelites and Pharaoh, king of Egypt: they were to bring the Israelites out of Egypt.
verses.tsw_comparator: The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them a command concerning the Israelites and Pharaoh king of Egypt: to bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt.

verses.rationale: Preserves the household introduction, firstborn rank, all four sons, and the clan summary using names consistent with Genesis 46.
verses.before: These are the heads of their ancestral houses. The sons of Reuben, Israel’s firstborn: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. These are the clans of Reuben.
verses.after: These are the heads of their ancestral households. The sons of Reuben, Israel’s firstborn, were Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. These were the clans of Reuben.
verses.tsw_comparator: These are the heads of their ancestral houses. The sons of Reuben, Israel’s firstborn: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. These are the clans of Reuben.

verses.rationale: Retains all six names and Shaul’s specifically female Canaanite parentage, matching the earlier family record.
verses.before: The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman. These are the clans of Simeon.
verses.after: Simeon’s sons were Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, whose mother was a Canaanite. These were the clans of Simeon.
verses.tsw_comparator: The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman. These are the clans of Simeon.

verses.rationale: Keeps the generational introduction, the three branches, and Levi’s exact age without turning the list into a complete chronology.
verses.before: These are the names of the sons of Levi according to their generations: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. The years of Levi’s life were one hundred thirty-seven years.
verses.after: These are the names of Levi’s sons, listed by their generations: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Levi lived a hundred and thirty-seven years.
verses.tsw_comparator: These are the names of the sons of Levi according to their generations: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. The years of Levi’s life were one hundred thirty-seven years.

verses.rationale: Retains both sons and the clan qualification in a compact list sentence.
verses.before: The sons of Gershon: Libni and Shimei, according to their clans.
verses.after: Gershon’s sons were Libni and Shimei, by their clans.
verses.tsw_comparator: The sons of Gershon: Libni and Shimei, according to their clans.

verses.rationale: Keeps all four sons and distinguishes Kohath’s 133 years from the two 137-year lifespans nearby.
verses.before: The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. The years of Kohath’s life were one hundred thirty-three years.
verses.after: Kohath’s sons were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. Kohath lived a hundred and thirty-three years.
verses.tsw_comparator: The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. The years of Kohath’s life were one hundred thirty-three years.

verses.rationale: Retains both sons and the closing generational summary before the genealogy narrows to Amram.
verses.before: The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites according to their generations.
verses.after: Merari’s sons were Mahli and Mushi. These were Levi’s clans, listed by their generations.
verses.tsw_comparator: The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites according to their generations.

verses.rationale: Preserves the explicitly stated aunt relationship, the Aaron/Moses order, and Amram’s exact age without harmonizing the kinship with later marriage rules.
verses.before: Amram took Jochebed, his aunt, as his wife, and she bore Aaron and Moses to him. The years of Amram’s life were one hundred thirty-seven years.
verses.after: Amram married his aunt Jochebed. She bore him Aaron and Moses. Amram lived a hundred and thirty-seven years.
verses.tsw_comparator: Amram took Jochebed, his aunt, as his wife, and she bore Aaron and Moses to him. The years of Amram’s life were one hundred thirty-seven years.

verses.rationale: Keeps all three names as one branch of the genealogy without adding later events associated with Korah.
verses.before: The sons of Izhar: Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri.
verses.after: Izhar’s sons were Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri.
verses.tsw_comparator: The sons of Izhar: Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri.

verses.rationale: Retains the three sons and their stated parent, avoiding confusion with the preceding Izhar branch.
verses.before: The sons of Uzziel: Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri.
verses.after: Uzziel’s sons were Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri.
verses.tsw_comparator: The sons of Uzziel: Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri.

verses.rationale: Preserves the woman’s name, both identifying relationships, and all four sons in source order.
verses.before: Aaron took Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon, as his wife; and she bore Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar to him.
verses.after: Aaron married Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon. She bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
verses.tsw_comparator: Aaron took Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon, as his wife; and she bore Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar to him.

verses.rationale: Keeps all three sons and the clan summary without changing Assir into a descriptive epithet.
verses.before: The sons of Korah: Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. These are the clans of the Korahites.
verses.after: Korah’s sons were Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. These were the Korahite clans.
verses.tsw_comparator: The sons of Korah: Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. These are the clans of the Korahites.

verses.rationale: Retains the unnamed daughter as one of Putiel’s daughters, Eleazar’s parentage, Phinehas, and the ancestral-household conclusion.
verses.before: Eleazar son of Aaron took one of the daughters of Putiel as his wife, and she bore Phinehas to him. These are the heads of the ancestral houses of the Levites according to their clans.
verses.after: Eleazar, Aaron’s son, married one of Putiel’s daughters. She bore him Phinehas. These were the heads of the Levite ancestral households, by their clans.
verses.tsw_comparator: Eleazar son of Aaron took one of the daughters of Putiel as his wife, and she bore Phinehas to him. These are the heads of the ancestral houses of the Levites according to their clans.

verses.rationale: Keeps Aaron before Moses and retains the organized-hosts image, with its military coloring explained selectively.
verses.before: This is the Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said, “Bring the Israelites out from the land of Egypt according to their companies.”
verses.after: These were the Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said, “Bring the Israelites out of Egypt in their companies.”
verses.tsw_comparator: This is the Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said, “Bring the Israelites out from the land of Egypt according to their companies.”

verses.rationale: Preserves the repeated identification and reversal to Moses/Aaron order instead of deleting the genealogical bridge as redundant.
verses.before: They are the ones who spoke to Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring the Israelites out of Egypt. This is Moses and Aaron.
verses.after: They were the ones who spoke to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to bring the Israelites out of Egypt—this Moses and Aaron.
verses.tsw_comparator: They are the ones who spoke to Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring the Israelites out of Egypt. This is Moses and Aaron.

verses.rationale: Keeps the temporal clause open across the verse boundary, attached to verse 29 within one paragraph.
verses.before: Now on the day the LORD spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt,
verses.after: When the LORD spoke to Moses in Egypt,
verses.tsw_comparator: Now on the day the LORD spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt,

verses.rationale: Continues verse 28’s sentence while retaining the renewed self-identification and command to transmit all the words.
verses.before: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, “I am the LORD. Speak to Pharaoh king of Egypt everything that I am speaking to you.”
verses.after: he told him, “I am the LORD. Tell Pharaoh, king of Egypt, everything I tell you.”
verses.tsw_comparator: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying, “I am the LORD. Speak to Pharaoh king of Egypt everything that I am speaking to you.”

verses.rationale: Keeps the repeated uncircumcised-lips objection and the listening question rather than smoothing away the narrative’s return to the earlier exchange.
verses.before: Yet Moses said before the LORD, “Look, I am uncircumcised of lips; how then will Pharaoh listen to me?”
verses.after: But Moses answered the LORD, “My lips are uncircumcised. How will Pharaoh listen to me?”
verses.tsw_comparator: But Moses said before the LORD, “Look, I am uncircumcised of lips; how then will Pharaoh listen to me?”
